questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: If light travelling in a straight line bends by a small but fixed angle, it could be an instance of
options: dispersion
reflection
diffraction
refraction
questions.solution:
When light undergoes reflection, its path changes direction. For a given angle of incidence $i$, the angle of deviation is $\delta = 180^{{}^{{}^{\circ}}} - 2i$. By choosing an appropriate angle of incidence (such as grazing incidence where $i \to 90^{{}^{{}^{\circ}}}$), the deviation can be a small, fixed angle.

When light undergoes refraction through a thin prism, it deviates by a small, fixed angle given by $\delta = (\mu - 1)A$, where $\mu$ is the refractive index and $A$ is the angle of the prism.

Dispersion involves different wavelengths of light bending by different angles, meaning the angle of deviation is not fixed for a composite beam of light.

Diffraction involves the spreading of light around obstacles into a continuous range of angles to form a pattern, rather than bending a single ray by one fixed angle.

Therefore, the bending of light by a small but fixed angle can be an instance of either reflection or refraction.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: The image of an extended object, positioned perpendicular to the principal axis of a mirror, will be erect if
options: the object is real while the image is virtual
the object is virtual while the image is real
both the object and the image are virtual
both the object and the image are real
questions.solution:
The lateral magnification for a spherical or plane mirror is given by $m = -\dfrac{v}{u}$.

For an erect image, the magnification $m$ must be positive, which means $m > 0$.

$\Rightarrow -\dfrac{v}{u} > 0 \Rightarrow \dfrac{v}{u} < 0$

This implies that the object distance $u$ and the image distance $v$ must have opposite signs.

According to the Cartesian sign convention, a real object has $u < 0$ and a virtual object has $u > 0$. Similarly, a real image has $v < 0$ and a virtual image has $v > 0$.

Since $u$ and $v$ must have opposite signs, there are two valid conditions.

First condition: $u < 0$ (real object) and $v > 0$ (virtual image).

Second condition: $u > 0$ (virtual object) and $v < 0$ (real image).

Thus, an erect image is formed when the object is real while the image is virtual, or when the object is virtual while the image is real.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: A real image of a point object located on the principal axis is produced by a convex lens. If the upper half of the lens is coated black,
options: the intensity of the image decreases.
the image does not shift
the image shifts upward
the image shifts downward
questions.solution:
When the upper half of a convex lens is coated black, the lower half of the lens remains uncovered and continues to refract the light rays from the object to form the complete image.

Since the focal length and the position of the lens remain unchanged, the position of the image is unaffected according to the lens formula $\dfrac{1}{v} - \dfrac{1}{u} = \dfrac{1}{f}$. Thus, the image does not shift.

However, the amount of light passing through the lens is reduced to half. As a result, the intensity or brightness of the image decreases.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: With reference to a spherical mirror, which of the following do(es) not depend on whether the rays are paraxial or not?
options: Radius of curvature
Focus
Pole
Principal axis
questions.solution:
The radius of curvature, pole, and principal axis are intrinsic geometric properties of a spherical mirror. They are defined by the physical shape and structure of the mirror itself and are entirely independent of the incident light rays.

The focus, however, is the point where rays parallel to the principal axis converge (or appear to diverge from) after reflection. For paraxial rays (rays close to the principal axis), they converge at a single well-defined point called the principal focus. For marginal rays (rays far from the principal axis), they converge at different points closer to the pole, leading to spherical aberration. Thus, the position of the focus depends on whether the incident rays are paraxial or not.

Therefore, the radius of curvature, pole, and principal axis do not depend on the paraxial nature of the rays.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: Identify the correct statement among the following.
options: If the incident rays are converging, the object is real.
The image of a virtual object is defined as a virtual image.
If the final rays are converging, a real image is formed.
A virtual image implies that the corresponding object is virtual.
questions.solution:
An object is defined by the incident rays. If the incident rays diverge from a point, the object is real. If the incident rays converge towards a point, the object is virtual. Thus, converging incident rays correspond to a virtual object, making the first statement incorrect.

An image is defined by the emergent (reflected or refracted) rays. If the emergent rays converge to a point, they actually intersect and a real image is formed. If the emergent rays diverge, they appear to come from a point and a virtual image is formed. Therefore, if the final rays are converging, a real image is formed, making the third statement correct.

A virtual object can form a real image (for example, a plane mirror forms a real image of a virtual object), making the second statement incorrect.

A real object can form a virtual image (for example, a plane mirror forms a virtual image of a real object), making the fourth statement incorrect.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: Suppose three converging lenses $L_1$, $L_2$, and $L_3$ share an identical geometrical construction. The refractive indices of $L_1$ and $L_2$ are $\mu_1$ and $\mu_2$, respectively. As shown in the figure, the upper half of lens $L_3$ has a refractive index $\mu_1$, while the lower half has $\mu_2$. When placed in a specific position, lens $L_1$ forms an image of a point object $O$ at $O_1$, and lens $L_2$ placed in the same position forms an image at $O_2$. If lens $L_3$ is positioned at this same location,
options: a single image will be formed somewhere between $O_1$ and $O_2$.
an image will be formed at $O_1$.
a single image will be formed away from $O_2$.
an image will be formed at $O_2$.
questions.solution:
The focal length of a lens is given by the lens maker's formula:

$\dfrac{1}{f} = (\mu - 1)\left(\dfrac{1}{R_1} - \dfrac{1}{R_2}\right)$

For lens $L_1$ with refractive index $\mu_1$, the image of object $O$ is formed at $O_1$.

For lens $L_2$ with refractive index $\mu_2$, the image of object $O$ is formed at $O_2$.

Lens $L_3$ is composed of two halves: the upper half has a refractive index $\mu_1$ and the lower half has a refractive index $\mu_2$.

The upper half of $L_3$ will refract the light rays exactly as lens $L_1$ does, converging them to form an image at $O_1$.

The lower half of $L_3$ will refract the light rays exactly as lens $L_2$ does, converging them to form an image at $O_2$.

Since each half of the lens forms a complete image of the object independently (with reduced intensity), two distinct images will be formed: one at $O_1$ and another at $O_2$.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: A screen is located at a distance of $40 \text{ cm}$ from an illuminated object. A converging lens is placed between the object and the screen in an attempt to form an image of the object on the screen. If no such position can be found, the focal length of the lens
options: must not be less than $10 \text{ cm}$
must not be greater than $20 \text{ cm}$
must be less than $10 \text{ cm}$
must be greater than $10 \text{ cm}$
questions.solution:
Let the distance between the object and the screen be $D$, and the object distance from the lens be $x$.

The image distance from the lens is $D - x$.

Using the lens formula, $\dfrac{1}{v} - \dfrac{1}{u} = \dfrac{1}{f}$

$\dfrac{1}{D-x} - \dfrac{1}{-x} = \dfrac{1}{f}$

$\dfrac{x + D - x}{x(D-x)} = \dfrac{1}{f}$

$x^2 - Dx + Df = 0$

For a real position of the lens to exist, the roots of this quadratic equation must be real, which requires the discriminant to be greater than or equal to zero:

$D^2 - 4Df \ge 0 \Rightarrow D \ge 4f$

Since no such position can be found, the roots must be imaginary, which means:

$D < 4f$

Given $D = 40 \text{ cm}$, we have:

$40 < 4f \Rightarrow f > 10 \text{ cm}$

Therefore, the focal length of the lens must be greater than $10 \text{ cm}$.
